title: VI. Smerdyakov
paragraphs: Sure enough, he found his father still at the table. The house had a dining room, but as always the meal was laid in the drawing room, which was the biggest room and was furnished in a showy, old-fashioned way. Everything in it was white and very old, upholstered in worn red silky cloth. Mirrors with elaborate, old-style carved frames of white and gold hung between the windows. The walls were covered in white paper, torn in many places, and two large portraits hung on them. One showed some prince who had been governor of the district thirty years before. The other showed some bishop, also long dead. In the corner opposite the door stood several ikons, with a lamp burning in front of them from nightfall ... more to light the room than out of devotion. Fyodor Pavlovitch went to bed very late, at three or four in the morning. Until then he would pace the room in the night, or sit in an armchair and think. It had become a habit. Often he slept in the house entirely alone, having sent his servants off to the lodge. Usually, though, Smerdyakov stayed and slept on a bench in the hall.

By the time Alyosha came in, dinner was over, but coffee and preserves had been brought out. After dinner Fyodor Pavlovitch liked something sweet with his brandy. Ivan was still at the table, sipping coffee. The servants, Grigory and Smerdyakov, stood by. Masters and servants alike seemed to be in unusually high spirits. Fyodor Pavlovitch was roaring with laughter. Alyosha heard that shrill laugh, which he knew so well, before he even reached the room. By the sound of it he could tell that his father had got only as far as the good-humored stage and was nowhere near properly drunk.

“Here he is! Here he is!” yelled Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted to see Alyosha. “Come and join us. Sit down. Coffee’s a lenten dish, but it’s hot and it’s good. I won’t offer you brandy, you’re keeping the fast. But would you like some? No, I’d better give you a little of our famous liqueur. Smerdyakov, go to the cupboard, second shelf on the right. Here are the keys. Quick, now!”
Alyosha began to turn the liqueur down.
“Never mind. If you won’t, we will,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, beaming. “But hold on—have you eaten?”
“Yes,” answered Alyosha, who had in fact had only a piece of bread and a glass of kvas in the Father Superior’s kitchen. “I would like some hot coffee, though.”

“Bravo, my darling! He’ll take coffee. Does it need heating up? No, it’s boiling. Excellent coffee, too: Smerdyakov made it. My Smerdyakov’s an artist at coffee, and at fish patties, and at fish soup as well. You must come some day for the fish soup. Tell me ahead of time.... But wait a minute; didn’t I tell you this morning to come home with your mattress and pillow and everything? Did you bring your mattress? He he he!”
“No, I didn’t,” said Alyosha, smiling too.

“Ah, but you were scared, you were scared this morning, weren’t you? There, my darling, I could never do anything to hurt you. Do you know, Ivan, I can’t stand up to the way he looks you straight in the face and laughs? It sets me laughing all over. I’m so fond of him. Alyosha, let me give you my blessing—a father’s blessing.”
Alyosha got up, but Fyodor Pavlovitch had already changed his mind.

“No, no,” he said. “I’ll just make the sign of the cross over you for now. Sit still. We’ve got a treat for you, and in your own line, too. It’ll make you laugh. Balaam’s ass has started talking to us—and how he talks! How he talks!”

Balaam’s ass, it turned out, was the valet Smerdyakov. He was a young man of about twenty-four, remarkably unsociable and silent. This was not shyness or bashfulness. Quite the reverse: he was conceited and seemed to look down on everybody.

I have to stop here and say a few words about him. Grigory and Marfa had raised him, but the boy grew up “with no gratitude in him,” as Grigory put it. He was an unfriendly child who seemed to eye the world with suspicion. When he was little, he loved to hang cats and then bury them with great ceremony. He would put a sheet on as if it were a priest’s vestment, chant, and swing something over the dead cat as if it were a censer. He did all of this on the sly, in absolute secrecy. Grigory caught him at it once and gave him a good thrashing. The boy crept into a corner and sulked there for a week. “He doesn’t care about you or me, the little monster,” Grigory used to tell Marfa, “and he doesn’t care about anybody. Are you even a human being?” he said, addressing the boy himself. “You’re no human being. You grew out of the mildew in the bath-house.[2] That’s what you are.” Smerdyakov, as we learned later, never forgave him those words. Grigory taught him to read and write, and when the boy turned twelve he started on the Scriptures. But nothing came of it. At the second or third lesson the boy suddenly gave a grin.
“What are you smirking at?” asked Grigory, glaring at him over his spectacles.
“Nothing. God made light on the first day, and the sun and moon and stars on the fourth. So where did the light come from on the first day?”

Grigory was stunned. The boy looked at his teacher mockingly, with something almost patronizing in his face. Grigory lost his temper. “I’ll show you where!” he shouted, and gave the boy a hard slap across the cheek. The boy took it without a word, and went back to his corner for a few days. A week later he had his first fit of the illness that stayed with him for the rest of his life—epilepsy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard about it, his attitude to the boy changed at once. Before that, he had paid him no attention. He never scolded him, and whenever they met he gave him a kopeck. Sometimes, in a good mood, he would send the boy a sweet from his table. But the moment he learned of the illness, he took a lively interest in him. He called in a doctor and tried various cures, but the disease proved incurable. On average the fits came once a month, though the gaps between them varied. Their severity varied too, some light and some very bad. Fyodor Pavlovitch strictly forbade Grigory to beat the boy, and began letting him come upstairs. For a while he also forbade anyone to teach him anything at all. One day, when the boy was about fifteen, Fyodor Pavlovitch saw him hanging around the bookcase, reading the titles through the glass. Fyodor Pavlovitch owned quite a few books—over a hundred—but nobody had ever seen him read one. He handed Smerdyakov the bookcase key on the spot. “Go on, read. You can be my librarian. It’s better for you to sit and read than to loaf around the yard. Here, read this,” and Fyodor Pavlovitch gave him _Evenings in a Cottage near Dikanka_.
He read a little but didn’t like it. Not once did he smile, and in the end he frowned.
“What’s wrong? Isn’t it funny?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Smerdyakov said nothing.
“Answer me, you fool!”
“It’s all lies,” the boy mumbled, with a grin.
“Then go to the devil! You’ve got the soul of a lackey. Wait, here’s Smaragdov’s _Universal History_. That’s all true. Read that.”
But Smerdyakov did not get past ten pages of Smaragdov. He found it boring. So the bookcase was locked up again.

Not long after, Marfa and Grigory told Fyodor Pavlovitch that Smerdyakov was slowly turning extraordinarily fussy. He would sit down to his soup, pick up the spoon, and peer into the soup. He would bend over it, inspect it, scoop up a spoonful and hold it to the light.
“What is it? A beetle?” Grigory would ask.
“Maybe a fly,” Marfa remarked.

The finicky youth never answered, but he did the same with his bread, his meat, and everything else he ate. He would lift a piece on his fork to the light, examine it as if under a microscope, and only after long thought decide to put it in his mouth.
“Ach! Look at the airs of a fine gentleman!” Grigory muttered as he watched him.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard how Smerdyakov was turning out, he made up his mind to have him as his cook, and sent him to Moscow to train. He stayed there some years and came back strikingly changed in looks. He seemed extraordinarily old for his age. His face had gone wrinkled and yellow, and strangely unmanly. In character he seemed almost exactly as he had been before leaving. He was as unsociable as ever and showed not the slightest wish for company. In Moscow, too, as we heard afterwards, he had always kept silent. Moscow itself had little interest for him; he saw very little of it and noticed hardly anything. He went to the theater once, and came back quiet and put out by it. On the other hand, he returned to us from Moscow well dressed, in a clean coat and clean linen. Every day, without fail, he brushed his clothes with great care twice, and he loved cleaning his smart calf boots with a special English polish until they shone like mirrors. He turned out to be a first-rate cook. Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him a salary, and Smerdyakov spent nearly all of it on clothes, pomade, perfume and the like. But he seemed to hold women in just as much contempt as men. With them he was discreet, almost unapproachable. Fyodor Pavlovitch began to see him a little differently. The fits were coming more often, and on the days when he was ill Marfa cooked, which did not suit Fyodor Pavlovitch at all.
“Why are your fits getting worse?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch, eyeing his new cook sideways. “Do you want to get married? Shall I find you a wife?”

But Smerdyakov went pale with anger and gave no answer. Fyodor Pavlovitch walked away from him with an impatient wave of the hand. What mattered most was that he trusted Smerdyakov’s honesty absolutely. Once, when Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk, he dropped three hundred-rouble notes, which he had only just been paid, in the muddy courtyard. He didn’t notice they were gone until the next day, and was hurrying to turn out his pockets when he saw the notes lying on the table. How had they got there? Smerdyakov had picked them up and brought them in the day before.

“Well, my lad, I’ve never come across anyone like you,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said gruffly, and gave him ten roubles. I should add that he not only believed in his honesty but, for some reason, actually liked him, though the young man looked at him as sourly as at everyone else and never said a word. He rarely spoke at all. If anyone at that time had asked what interested the young man, or what went on in his head, you could not have told by looking at him. And yet he would sometimes stop short in the house, or even out in the yard or the street, and stand there for ten minutes, deep in thought. Anyone who studied faces would have said that his held no thought, no reflection, only a kind of contemplation. There is a remarkable painting by Kramskoy called “Contemplation.” It shows a forest in winter and, on a road through the forest, in total solitude, a peasant in a ragged kaftan and bark shoes. He seems lost in thought. But he is not thinking; he is “contemplating.” If someone touched him, he would give a start and look at them like a man waking up, bewildered. True, he would come to himself at once; but if you asked what he had been thinking about, he would remember nothing. Yet he most likely carries within him, hidden away, the impression that held him in those moments. Those impressions are precious to him, and no doubt he stores them up without noticing, even without knowing it. How and why, naturally, he doesn’t know either. After storing up impressions for many years, he may suddenly drop everything and go on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to save his soul, or perhaps he will suddenly burn down his own village, or perhaps do both. There are a good many “contemplatives” among the peasantry. Well, Smerdyakov was probably one of them, and he was probably greedily storing up his impressions, hardly knowing why.
